Bear Lake sculpin (Cottus extensus) hatch from demersal, adhesive eggs that are deposited in concealed nests beneath cobble substrate in the cold, well-oxygenated waters of Bear Lake. Following eclosion, the prolarvae emerge as tiny, yolk-dependent organisms that remain on the spawning grounds, absorbing their endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. At the moment of hatching, these newly emerged larvae weigh just 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams], a minuscule mass that is typical of cottid fry and necessitates a rich supply of interstitial zooplankton to support early growth. First feeding commences shortly after yolk-sac resorption, at which point the free-swimming larvae begin actively capturing small copepods and cladocerans. The incubation period is strongly temperature-dependent, and in Bear Lake, where water temperatures consistently hover near 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the egg stage can last several weeks before chorion rupture occurs and the alevins enter the water column.

As juveniles grow and approach the onset of gonadal recrudescence, the total length at which puberty is attained appears to be remarkably similar between the sexes. Field surveys of maturing individuals have demonstrated that both females and males reach sexual maturity at a total length of 5.75 centimeters [Lp = 5.75 centimeters], a value that is relatively small compared to many other benthic sculpins and suggests an early investment in reproductive effort. At this same length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty for both females and males has been measured at approximately 2.089 grams [Wwp = approximately 2.089 grams]. This synchrony in size at maturity between the sexes is somewhat unusual among freshwater cottids, where males often mature at a slightly larger body size due to the demands of nest guarding. The consistency of these estimates, derived from histological examination of gonad tissue, indicates that both sexes follow a similar growth trajectory during the sub-adult phase prior to their first spawning event.

Reproductive activity in Bear Lake sculpin is tightly synchronized with the cold thermal regime characteristic of their deep-lake habitat. At the stable temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], which prevails in the hypolimnion during the spawning season, females of approximately 9.5 centimeters total length display a notable level of fecundity. Specifically, a female of this size will produce roughly 486 eggs per year [Ri = roughly 486 eggs per year] when the full reproductive period is integrated across the entire year. This rate is derived from a fecundity-length relationship that indicates rapidly increasing egg production with body size. The reproductive frequency, in this case, is best interpreted as a continuous daily output over the spawning season rather than discrete clutches, reflecting the protracted, batch-spawning strategy observed in many deep-water cottids. This strategy ensures that larvae emerge over an extended period, buffering against stochastic variation in prey availability following the onset of exogenous feeding.

The asymptotic body sizes achieved by adult Bear Lake sculpin differ substantially between the sexes, a pattern that is consistent with the species' polygynous mating system and the energetic demands of parental care. Females, which invest heavily in egg production, attain a maximum total length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters] in the wild, corresponding to an ultimate wet weight of 26.6 grams [Wwi = 26.6 grams]. Males, by contrast, do not grow as large, with the largest recorded individuals reaching a total length of 12 centimeters [Li = 12 centimeters] and a final adult body mass of 20.7 grams [Wwi = 20.7 grams]. This dimorphism in ultimate size is likely driven by the competing demands of nest defense and foraging efficiency; males must remain agile enough to guard territories among the cobble substrate, while females channel surplus energy into somatic growth to maximize fecundity. The length-mass relationship underlying these estimates conforms to a power-law scaling typical of benthic fishes.

Longevity data for Bear Lake sculpin, derived from otolith-based age estimation of the oldest individuals collected during population surveys, indicate a maximum lifespan of 4 years [am = 4 years] under the prevailing thermal conditions of their native environment, where water temperatures remain near 7 °C [T = 7 °C] for much of the year. This relatively short life span, when compared to other cold-water fishes, reflects a life-history strategy oriented toward rapid maturation and early, intense reproduction over a few spawning seasons. The combination of small body size, early maturity at 5.75 centimeters [Lp = 5.75 centimeters] total length, and a compressed adult life span suggests that Cottus extensus operates under strong selection for high annual reproductive output to compensate for elevated mortality rates during the larval and juvenile stages. This pace of life is characteristic of many cottid species inhabiting unproductive, oligotrophic lakes where food resources are seasonally pulsed and unpredictable.
